Full text

Abstract

Life satisfaction is widely used as a primary indicator of population wellbeing in research and policymaking. Yet it remains unclear which wellbeing domains contribute to life satisfaction and other global life evaluations. In a UK sample (N = 1,050), we examined how four global measures (Satisfaction With Life Scale, single-item life satisfaction, Cantril's Ladder, a good life evaluation) reflected experiences across 15 wellbeing domains. Machine learning analyses identified optimism, personal circumstances, happiness, and meaning and purpose as the strongest predictors, with other domains contributing little predictive information.

Crucially, domains' contributions corresponded only weakly with participants' domain importance ratings, challenging the assumption that unequal contributions of domains reflect what people value most. Global life evaluations thus appear to provide selectively weighted rather than comprehensive summaries of wellbeing, potentially underrepresenting certain domains people consider important. Researchers and policymakers seeking comprehensive or value-based assessments could therefore complement global measures with multidimensional assessments.

[div-01]

Global life evaluations, particularly life satisfaction measures, are widely used to monitor societal progress and guide public policy (Fabian & Pykett, 2022; Frijters et al., 2020). Such measures ask individuals to evaluate their lives as a whole rather than specific aspects of their wellbeing (Clark et al., 2018). Yet, wellbeing is generally conceptualized as a multifaceted construct, encompassing domains ranging from affective states and relationships to meaning, autonomy, and personal growth (Linton et al., 2016; VanderWeele & Johnson, 2025). Understanding which wellbeing domains global life evaluations reflect-and whether these correspond to what people themselves consider important -is therefore critical to their scientific and policy use.

The Multifaceted Nature of Wellbeing

Despite considerable differences, theoretical frameworks generally converge in treating wellbeing as multidimensional (Iasiello et al., 2024). Synthesizing this literature, Iasiello and colleagues (2024, 2026) identified recurring domains, including autonomy, competence, engagement, meaning, personal growth, personal relationships, and selfacceptance. Considering the lack of consensus about which domains should constitute wellbeing, global life evaluation measures offer an appealing alternative: They appear to circumvent decisions about which domains to include and how to weigh them (Helliwell et al., 2026).

Life Satisfaction as a Democratic, All-Encompassing Measure

Life satisfaction has been defined as a "report of how a respondent evaluates or appraises his or her life taken as a whole. It is intended to represent a broad, reflective appraisal that a person makes of his or her life" (Diener, 2006, p. 401). Accordingly, global life evaluations are often treated as summary indicators potentially capturing diverse wellbeing dimensions within a single assessment (Diener, 2006). This approach has been characterized as a 'democratic' measure of wellbeing (Clark et al., 2018; Vittersø, 2025): Rather than imposing researcher-defined domains and weights, global evaluations are assumed to allow respondents to integrate the aspects of life they personally value into an overall evaluation (Diener & Tov, 2012; Oishi, 2012). Consistent with conceptualizations of wellbeing as personally valued fulfillment (Disabato et al., 2025; DeYoung & Tiberius, 2023), this suggests that more important domains should contribute more strongly to global evaluations. Relatedly, life satisfaction may involve comparing one's actual circumstances with personal ideals (Diener et al., 1985; Pavot & Diener, 1993), as reflected in the Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS) items, such as "In most ways my life is close to my ideal." Thus, global life evaluations may reflect not only how people are doing across domains, but also how their experiences compare with their ideals and how much those domains matter to them.

Emerging evidence, however, suggests that wellbeing domains are unevenly represented in global evaluations. Life satisfaction correlates only modestly with some multidimensional wellbeing measures (Joshanloo et al., 2019; Vittersø et al., 2009) and classifications of flourishing differ depending on whether global or multidimensional measures are used (Huppert & So, 2013). More specifically, Cantril's Ladder, which asks respondents to rate their lives from worst to best possible, appears to reflect considerations of power and wealth more strongly than harmony and social relationships (Nilsson et al., 2024).

Similarly, single-item life satisfaction shows stronger associations with hedonic aspects such as pleasure than eudaimonic aspects such as development, social care, and justice (Vittersø et al., 2009; Vittersø & Teulings, 2025).

However, uneven associations with wellbeing domains are not necessarily inconsistent with the democratic account: They could simply reflect differences in what people value. If respondents prioritize personally important domains, those domains should contribute more strongly to their global evaluations. Initial evidence nevertheless suggests that domains most strongly associated with life satisfaction diverge from respondents' importance ratings (Vittersø & Teulings, 2025). However, this study examined only a limited set of domains and a single life satisfaction measure, leaving unclear whether this discrepancy generalizes to a broader wellbeing domains and other global evaluations.

Present Study

Recent calls to prioritize single-item global evaluations over multidimensional assessments underscore the need to establish what these measures truly capture (Helliwell et al., 2026). Here, we address this gap by using machine learning to examine how four global life evaluation measures reflect experiences across 15 wellbeing domains. First, we estimated domains' relative contributions to predicting global life evaluations across several measures. Second, we compared these predictive contributions with participants' importance ratings of these domains. Finally, we examined whether discrepancies between experienced and ideal wellbeing, and self-reported domain importance, improved prediction beyond experienced wellbeing alone.

Research Transparency Statement

General Disclosures

Conflicts

Study Disclosures

Preregistration: The study, including our research questions and analysis plan, was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) at https://osf.io/nxmjw. Deviations from the preregistration are reported in the Online Supplementary Materials (OSM) Section 1. Materials: All study materials are available at OSM Table S2. Data: This study's data, analysis code, and supplementary materials are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23983373?utm_source=chatgpt.com.

Method

Participants and Procedure

We used Prolific to collect data from a nationally representative sample of 1,050 UKbased participants (Mage = 46.48, SDage = 15.71; 50.5% women). Our sample size was comparable to previous studies with continuous outcomes and a similar number of candidate predictors (Basterfield & Newman, 2025; Panicheva et al., 2022; Pearson et al., 2019), supporting the use of our prediction models. Table S1 in the OSM provides detailed sample characteristics.

Participants first completed the global life evaluation measures before responding to questions about specific wellbeing domains, to avoid influencing their global evaluations by making particular domains salient. The order of measures within each block was randomized across participants. Participants then rated the importance of each wellbeing domain and, lastly, provided demographic information. Upon completion, participants were compensated in line with Prolific's guidelines for ethical pay (i.e., £9.44 per hour). To assess data quality, we flagged participants (a) who failed both attention checks (N = 3) and (b) gave the same response to more than nine consecutive items (N = 190). We retained these participants in the primary analyses and conducted sensitivity analyses excluding them to assess the robustness of our findings.

Measures

Global Life Evaluation Measures

We assessed global life evaluations using four instruments: the 5-item Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS; Diener et al., 1985), a single-item life satisfaction measure (LS1; OECD, 2013), Cantril's Ladder (CL; Cantril, 1965), and a good life evaluation (GL; Bjørndal et al., 2026).

Domain-Specific Wellbeing

To assess domain-specific wellbeing, we used items from the Positive Mental Health Taxonomy (Iasiello et al., 2025), covering autonomy, calmness, competence, development, engagement, happiness, meaning and purpose, optimism, personal circumstances, personal relationships, physical health, self-acceptance, sense of community, and self-congruence 1.

We selected three items per domain from the taxonomy and complemented these with three prosociality items adapted from earlier work (Hanel et al., 2024; MASKED FOR REVIEW).

For each item, participants reported to what extent they had experienced this aspect in their current lives during the past two weeks (experienced wellbeing). Following earlier work ([MASKED FOR REVIEW]), we additionally used parallel items to assess the extent to which participants would prefer to experience each aspect in their ideal life (ideal wellbeing).

Domain Importance Ratings

We assessed domain importance by asking participants to rate how important each of the 15 wellbeing domains (e.g., "Feeling calm and at peace") was for their personal wellbeing currently.

Demographics

1 To maintain focus on core wellbeing domains, we did not include items from the activities and functioning, body image, coping, spirituality, or vitality dimensions. Additionally, we excluded the life satisfaction domain to avoid conceptual and linguistic overlap with global life evaluation measures.

Lastly, participants reported their age, gender, birth country, residence country, education, employment status, political orientation, and subjective socioeconomic status using McArthur's ladder (Adler et al., 2000).

Statistical Analyses

Pre-processing

The five SWLS items were averaged to create a composite score. For each domaindomain, experienced and ideal wellbeing scores were calculated by averaging their respective three items. Domain-level gap scores were calculated by averaging the absolute discrepancies between ideal and experienced wellbeing for each item, with higher scores indicating greater discrepancies from one's ideals. We also calculated means, standard deviations, and correlations for the global life evaluation measures, domain-specific measures, and domain importance ratings (see OSM Section 4).

Machine Learning Analyses

To examine the relative weighting of specific wellbeing domains in global evaluations, we first fit random forest models, tree-based machine learning methods that flexibly capture nonlinear relationships and interactions among predictors and are generally robust to multicollinearity (Breiman, 2001; Hastie et al., 2009). Random forest models were estimated using the ranger package (version 0.17.0; Wright & Ziegler, 2017), with 500 trees (i.e., individual predictors fitted on a subset of both participants and input variables). We then used SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values to estimate each domain's relative contribution to model predictions (using fastshap, version 0.1.1; Greenwell, 2024; Lundberg & Lee, 2017). To express these contributions as percentages, we divided each domain's mean absolute SHAP value by the sum of mean absolute SHAP values across all domains and multiplied by 100. To assess the correspondence between model-based feature importance and self-reported domain importance, we calculated Pearson and Spearman correlations across the 15 domains for each global life evaluation measure. Together, these analyses identified which domains contributed most strongly to predictions of global life evaluations.

We next used LASSO regression to examine if representing wellbeing as discrepancies between participants' ideal and experienced wellbeing improved prediction relative to experienced wellbeing alone and whether incorporating self-reported domain importance provided additional predictive information. LASSO applies an L1 penalty that shrinks regression coefficients toward zero, thereby performing automatic variable selection and reducing overfitting (Hastie et al., 2009; Tibshirani, 1996). For each global life evaluation measure, we fit three separate models incorporating 1) experienced wellbeing, 2) discrepancies between ideal and experienced wellbeing (gap scores), and 3) gap scores combined with self-reported domain importance ratings. To examine the incremental predictive value of weaker domains and their predictive performance when considered separately from stronger domains, we additionally conducted exploratory analyses comparing the predictive performance of models including all 15 experienced wellbeing domains with models restricted to the strongest and weakest domains, as identified in the random forest analyses. Then, to examine whether a more granular measurement level provided additional predictive information, we repeated the same procedure using item-level predictors. All predictors were standardized and predictive performance was estimated using 10-fold nested cross-validation (using glmnet, version 4.1.8; Friedman et al., 2010). Performance across the estimated models was compared using out-of-sample predictive accuracy, including R² , root mean squared error (RMSE), and correlations between predicted and observed scores. All analyses were conducted in R (version 4.3.2; R Core Team, 2023).

Results

Descriptive Results

Overall, participants reported varying levels of wellbeing across both global (MSWLS = 4.32; MLS1 = 6.23; MCL = 5.91; Mgoodlife = 5.23; see Figure S1 for distributions) and domainspecific wellbeing measures (Mpooled = 59.3; see Figure S2 and Table S3). Experienced wellbeing varied considerably across domains, with participants reporting the highest levels for physical health (M = 71.1) and the lowest for community wellbeing (M = 41.3). The average discrepancy between experienced and ideal wellbeing also varied substantially across domains, with community showing the largest gap (M = 38.5) and personal relationships the smallest (M = 19.4).

For domain importance, participants rated all domains as relatively important (Mpooled = 82.9, SD = 19.1), with physical health rated as most important (M = 92.1) and somewhat lower ratings for development (M = 67.7) and community (M = 66.5). Figure 1 provides an overview of the gap between participants' experienced and ideal wellbeing within each domain, alongside the importance they assigned to each domain. Bivariate correlations across domain-level wellbeing and global wellbeing are reported in Figures S4-S5 and item-level descriptive and correlational results in Figure S3 and Tables S4-S6.

Figure 1 Domain Importance Ratings and Average Domain Gaps

Note. Domain importance ratings were reported on a 0-100 scale, and gap scores were scaled to range from 0-100; axis ranges were adjusted to improve visual interpretability. Dashed lines represent the mean values across domains for gap scores and importance ratings, thereby dividing the plot into four quadrants: dark green indicates higher importance and smaller gaps; dark blue, higher importance and larger gaps; light green, lower importance and smaller gaps; and light blue, lower importance and larger gaps.

Domains' Feature Importance

We investigated the role of each wellbeing domain in global life evaluations using random forest models and SHAP values. Figure 2 presents SHAP values across global outcomes, with larger absolute values indicating stronger contributions to model predictions.

Figure 3 provides an overview of domains' contribution profiles with a ranking of domains based on their predictive contribution per outcome.

Across all global life evaluation measures, the optimism domain showed the largest SHAP values and the widest distributions (see Figure 2 and 3), accounting for 19.0-21.6% of total feature attribution. Beyond optimism, personal circumstances, happiness, and meaning and purpose consistently emerged as strong contributors. Personal relationships, autonomy, and self-acceptance, showed more modest predictive contributions, followed by selfcongruence. In contrast, engagement, physical health, calmness, competence, community, development, and prosociality showed relatively small SHAP values clustering around zero, indicating that these domains made relatively small contributions to model predictions. Both the magnitude (Figure 2) and relative ordering of domains' contributions (Figure 3) were highly similar across the four global life evaluation measures, pointing to a largely shared domain-contribution profile.

Within this broad similarity, Cantril's Ladder showed a slightly more distinct profile.

In particular, personal circumstances contributed relatively strongly to Cantril's Ladder (17.4% of total feature attribution) compared to the other measures (11.8%-13.7%), suggesting that in comparison to other global evaluations, responses to Cantril's Ladder may rely more heavily on evaluations of one's life circumstances such as living conditions, responsibilities, and standard of living. Nevertheless, these differences were small and the overall pattern remained highly consistent across measures. Domains' Feature Importance Across Global Life Evaluation Measures Note. Each dot represents one participant. Colors indicate domain-specific wellbeing levels, ranging from relatively low (blue) to high (red). Larger absolute SHAP values indicate stronger contributions to the predicted global life evaluations. Domains are ordered by their pooled mean absolute SHAP values across all global life evaluation measures. Note. Domains are ranked within each global life evaluation measure based on their mean absolute SHAP values. Colors represent each domain's pooled mean absolute SHAP value across the four measures.

Domain Importance: Machine Learning vs Self-Reported

We then compared the model-based importance of wellbeing domains with participants' self-reported domain importance ratings. Figure 4 plots each domain's share of total absolute SHAP attribution against its average self-reported importance rating for each global life evaluation measure. Overall, model-based and self-reported domain importance showed only partial correspondence, with modest Pearson correlations (r = .29-.32) and weaker rank-order correlations (Spearman's ρ = .11-.25) across measures. Optimism, personal circumstances, happiness, and meaning and purpose generally showed both high predictive contributions and high self-reported importance. However, several other domains, including physical health, prosociality, self-congruence, competence, and engagement, were rated as similarly important by participants but accounted for substantially smaller shares of model attribution. Thus, whereas participants rated most wellbeing domains as relatively important, their contributions to predicted global life evaluations varied considerably.

Together, these findings suggest that global life evaluations give unequal weight to different wellbeing domains and that this weighting corresponds only partially with the importance participants themselves assign to those domains.

Figure 4

Model-Based Feature Importance and Self-Reported Domain Importance Note. Abbreviations: Aut = autonomy, calm = calmness, comp = competence, dev = development, eng = engagement, happ = happiness, mean = meaning and purpose, opt = optimism, perscirc = personal circumstances, persrel = personal relationships, health = physical health, pros = prosociality, selfacc = self-acceptance, comm = sense of community, selfcon = self-congruence. Domain importance ratings were reported on a 0-100 scale; the axis range was adjusted to improve visual interpretability. To facilitate comparisons of domains' relative contributions across outcomes, mean absolute SHAP values were normalized within each model by dividing each domain's mean absolute SHAP value by the sum of mean absolute SHAP values across all domains and multiplying by 100.

Model Performance: Do Ideal-Experienced Gaps and Self-Reported Domain Importance Improve Predictions?

We next examined whether incorporating participants' ideal wellbeing levels and selfreported domain importance into our models improved their ability to predict global life evaluations. We next examined whether global life evaluations were better predicted by experienced wellbeing, discrepancies between ideal and experienced wellbeing (gap scores), or gap scores combined with self-reported domain importance ratings. Across all four global life evaluation measures, models based on experienced wellbeing showed the best out-ofsample predictive performance (see Figure 5). Predictive performance was strongest for LS1, accounting for 66.6% of the variance in out-of-sample scores (R² = .666, RMSE = 1.25, rpredobs = .816). Model performance was similarly strong for SWLS (R² = .596, RMSE = 0.905, rpred-obs = .772) and the good life measure (R² = .598, RMSE = 0.863, rpred-obs = .773), and somewhat lower for Cantril's Ladder (R² = .505, RMSE = 1.20, rpred-obs = .710). Thus, replacing experienced wellbeing with ideal-experienced gaps, either alone or in combination with participants' domain importance ratings, did not improve predictive performance.

To examine whether a more fine-grained representation of domain-specific wellbeing improved predictions, we repeated these analyses using item-level rather than domain-level predictors. Item-level models showed no substantial improvements in out-of-sample predictive performance relative to domain-level models (see Figure 5; e.g., for experienced wellbeing: ΔR 2 pooled = .038, ΔRMSE pooled = -.049, Δrpred-obs, pooled = .025). Retaining item-level information thus provided little additional predictive value beyond the aggregated domain scores, supporting our domain-level analytical approach. Note. Model 1 included experienced wellbeing scores; Model 2 included ideal-experienced wellbeing gap scores; Model 3 included idealexperienced wellbeing gap scores and domain importance ratings. Dots represent pooled out-of-sample R² values from nested cross-validation. Error bars indicate variability across outer folds.

In exploratory analyses, we examined how predictive performance changed when restricting experienced wellbeing predictors to different subsets of domains based on their SHAP contributions. These comparisons allowed us to examine both the incremental predictive value of weaker domains as well as their predictive performance when modeled separately from stronger domains. Excluding the seven weakest predictors (calm, community, competence, development, engagement, physical health, and prosociality) resulted in negligible reductions in out-of-sample predictive performance (ΔR² = -.002 to -.009 across measures, see Figure 6). Even when retaining only the four strongest predictors (optimism, personal circumstances, happiness, and meaning and purpose), models retained 97.8-99.1% of the full 15-domain models' predictive R² (ΔR² = -.005 to -.013). However, models containing only the seven weakest predictors still explained substantial variance in global life evaluations (R² = .364-.507), although considerably less than models containing the strongest domains. Together, these findings indicate that domains with smaller SHAP contributions are not necessarily weak predictors of global evaluations, but contribute relatively little additional predictive information beyond that captured by stronger domains.

Figure 6

Predictive Performance Across Different Sets of Experienced Wellbeing Domains Note. Out-of-sample predictive performance of LASSO models using different subsets of experienced wellbeing domains across four global life evaluation measures. Predictor subsets were defined based on domains' relative contributions in the Random Forest analyses. The top-four model included optimism, personal circumstances, happiness, and meaning and purpose; the top-eight model additionally included personal relationships, autonomy, self-acceptance, and self-congruence. The bottom-seven model included the seven domains with the smallest SHAP contributions.

Sensitivity Analyses

First, we ran a robustness check excluding participants flagged for potential inattentiveness. Results remained substantively unchanged, suggesting that the findings were not impacted when accounting for potentially inattentive responding (see OSM Section 5 and Figures S6-S8).

As a supplementary test of whether selective domain weighting is specific to global life evaluations or characterizes global wellbeing measures more broadly, we also examined conceptually distinct global measures of happiness and meaning. We observed similar patterns of selective domain weighting, with optimism remaining the strongest predictor across measures. However, the relative contributions of other domains varied, suggesting that selective weighting extends beyond global life evaluations, while the specific domains emphasized partly depend on the construct being assessed (see OSM Section 6 and Figures S9-S10).

Discussion

Although wellbeing is widely conceptualized as a multidimensional construct (Linton et al., 2016; VanderWeele & Johnson, 2025), it is commonly assessed using global life evaluations such as life satisfaction. We investigated how four global life evaluation measures reflected 15 wellbeing domains and whether their predictive contributions aligned with self-reported domain importance. Across measures, optimism, personal circumstances, happiness, and meaning and purpose contributed most strongly to predictions, whereas other domains (calmness, community, competence, development, engagement, physical health, prosociality, and self-congruence) contributed comparatively little. Importantly, this unequal weighting corresponded only partially with participants' stated domain importance. Together, our findings suggest that global life evaluations provide selective rather than comprehensive summaries of multidimensional wellbeing.

Global Life Evaluations Reflect Wellbeing Domains Unevenly

Our findings extend previous evidence of unequal domain representation in singleitem life satisfaction (Vittersø & Teulings, 2025) and Cantril's Ladder (Nilsson et al., 2024).

In line with previous work, our findings suggest that life satisfaction judgments reflect "spontaneous good-bad evaluations", relying on familiar and easily accessible information, rather than comprehensively integrated assessments of all relevant life domains (Vittersø, 2025). Consistent with this perspective, we found that the strongest predictors related to optimism, personal circumstances (e.g., living conditions), happiness, and experienced meaning. The contribution of personal circumstances is particularly noteworthy given that material and structural conditions are often overlooked in multidimensional wellbeing frameworks, despite evidence that people consider them essential for flourishing (Willen et al., 2022). Other domains, including social, developmental, and prosocial functioning, contributed less. Recent meta-analytic evidence similarly demonstrated that life satisfaction is most strongly associated with emotional functioning and psychological resources (Simonsmeier et al., 2026). Although our analyses cannot establish the cognitive processes underlying global evaluations, our findings support recent critiques of the assumption that life satisfaction functions as a broad, balanced evaluation of life "as a whole" (Fabian et al., 2026; Vittersø, 2025).

Across the four global life evaluation measures, domain-contribution patterns were largely consistent, with only minor differences (e.g., a stronger contribution of personal circumstances to Cantril's Ladder). Supplementary analyses of global happiness and meaning likewise revealed selective domain weighting, suggesting that this pattern may characterize global wellbeing measures more generally, although the strongest contributing domains may vary across measures.

Domain Contributions Do Not Consistently Reflect People's Priorities

A central finding was the limited correspondence between domains' predictive contributions to global evaluations and their self-reported importance. Although participants considered most wellbeing domains relatively important, contributions to global life evaluations differed considerably. Physical health, prosociality, self-congruence, competence, and engagement received high importance ratings but contributed relatively little to model predictions. This discrepancy challenges a central assumption underlying the characterization of life satisfaction as a "democratic" wellbeing measure (Clark et al., 2018; Helliwell et al., 2026). According to this account, global evaluations allow individuals to determine which aspects of life matter most, avoiding researcher-imposed domains or weights. Unequal domain contributions would therefore not necessarily be problematic if they reflected respondents' own priorities. Our findings, however, suggest that predictive contributions do not consistently correspond with the importance individuals explicitly assign to different domains. This distinction is especially relevant given evidence that people across cultures place considerable value on health, relationships, meaning, happiness, and being a good person (Lomas et al., 2026). Although some of these domains contributed strongly to global evaluations, others (particularly community, physical health, and prosociality) contributed comparatively little. Consequently, global evaluations may underrepresent aspects of wellbeing that people nevertheless consider important to their wellbeing.

Importantly, self-reported importance ratings may not fully capture the criteria individuals actually use when evaluating their lives. People may implicitly prioritize certain domains, or their judgments may be influenced by accessibility, affective salience, or other cognitive processes. Moreover, domains with weak predictive contributions such as prosociality may influence global life evaluations indirectly through happiness or meaning, potentially obscuring its unique predictive contribution. Our findings therefore do not rule out the possibility that global evaluations reflect personally meaningful considerations. Rather, they challenge the assumption that these measures reliably integrate wellbeing domains according to individuals' explicitly stated priorities.

The Role of Ideal Wellbeing States and Domain Importance in Global Evaluations

Experienced wellbeing across the 15 domains explained substantial variation in global life evaluations. Predictive performance was strongest for single-item life satisfaction and weakest for Cantril's Ladder, consistent with recent findings (Marquez et al., 2026; Padgett et al., 2025). However, representing wellbeing as discrepancies between experienced and ideal states did not improve prediction relative to experienced wellbeing alone, even when incorporating self-reported domain importance. These findings provide limited support for theoretical accounts emphasizing comparisons between actual circumstances and personally held ideals or standards in life satisfaction judgments (Diener et al., 1985; Pavot & Diener, 1993). Instead, participants' reported experiences across wellbeing domains predicted their global evaluations more accurately than the extent to which these experiences matched their ideals. Nevertheless, this does not establish that individuals' ideals or values play no role in global evaluations, only that explicitly measured discrepancies and importance ratings added little predictive information beyond experienced wellbeing.

Implications for Wellbeing Measurement

Global life evaluations capture substantial variation in domain-specific wellbeing and offer practical advantages as concise, easily administered measures. However, their selective domain weighting means that they should not automatically be interpreted as comprehensive assessments of multidimensional wellbeing or as summaries reflecting individuals' stated priorities.

These findings inform ongoing debates about global versus multidimensional wellbeing measurement. Whereas VanderWeele and Johnson (2025) and Ruggeri and colleagues (2020, 2026) emphasize the importance of assessing distinct wellbeing domains, Helliwell and colleagues (2026) argue that global evaluations allow individuals to evaluate their lives according to personally meaningful criteria without researcher-imposed domains or weights. Our results support elements of both perspectives: Global evaluations provide informative overall assessments, but domains contribute unevenly and only partially in accordance with self-reported importance.

The appropriate measurement strategy therefore depends on the research or policy objective. Global measures remain valuable for monitoring overall life evaluations at the population level. However, when evaluating interventions, identifying areas requiring improvement, or monitoring aspects of life people consider important, global evaluations alone may be insufficient. Complementing them with domain-specific assessments could help identify which aspects of wellbeing change and provide a more comprehensive picture of population wellbeing.

Limitations and Future Directions

Several limitations warrant consideration. First, our sample was drawn exclusively from the United Kingdom. As wellbeing conceptions and priorities vary across cultures (Joshanloo, 2014; Krys et al., 2021 Krys et al., , 2023 Krys et al., , 2024;; Oishi et al., 2013), cross-cultural replication is needed to establish the generalizability of these patterns. Second, our domains, derived from recent taxonomic work (Iasiello et al., 2026), were not necessarily exhaustive and omitted domains may contribute to global evaluations. Finally, our analyses identified predictive associations rather than the cognitive processes underlying global judgments.

Recent studies suggest substantial heterogeneity in how respondents interpret and answer global wellbeing questions (Benjamin et al., 2023; Fabian et al., 2026). Experimental research could investigate which domains individuals spontaneously consider, how reflection influences their evaluations, and whether these processes correspond with stated priorities.

Longitudinal research could further examine whether changes in specific domains predict subsequent changes in global evaluations, including potential indirect relationships. Largescale international datasets could facilitate such investigations across populations and over time.

Conclusion

Global life evaluations provide informative but selectively weighted summaries of wellbeing. Across measures, a relatively small subset of domains contributed most strongly to predictions, while several domains participants considered important were comparatively weak predictors. These findings challenge the assumption that global evaluations necessarily reflect the aspects of wellbeing people value most. As such measures increasingly inform research and public policy, complementing them with multidimensional assessments may provide a more comprehensive picture of how people are doing across the wellbeing domains they consider important.
